depth.correction: `const T *` only stops you writing through that pointer; other code may still change the value. `&T` also guarantees that nothing mutates the value while the borrow is in use (outside interior-mutability types such as `Cell`), which is why the compiler can reject the `push`.

title: Pointers to References

writing.summary: A reference is a pointer the compiler checks: shared `&T` for reading, or one exclusive `&mut T` for writing, never both at once.
writing.rule: At any point a value has either any number of shared borrows `&T` or exactly one mutable borrow `&mut T`, never both; a borrow lends access without transferring ownership.
writing.explanation:
The C program keeps `int *first` into a dynamic array and then pushes. `realloc` may move the buffer, so `first` can dangle: AddressSanitizer reports `heap-use-after-free`, while a plain build may print the right number by luck. The bug is not the pointer itself but the combination of a reader that keeps a pointer and a writer that changes the buffer it points into.

Rust references are pointers with two rules that the compiler enforces. `&T` is shared: any number may exist, and none of them can mutate the value. It is like `const T *`, plus the guarantee that nobody else mutates the value while the borrow is in use. `&mut T` is exclusive: while it is in use, no other reference to the value may be used, which is what C's `restrict` promises and never checks. `v.push(2)` needs `&mut v`, so with `first = &v[0]` still in use, rustc reports `E0502`.

A borrow lasts until its last use, not until the end of the scope. Moving the `println!` above the push, or copying the `i32` out with `let first = v[0];`, removes the conflict. References are never null and always point at a live value, so the defensive `if (!p) return -1;` at the top of a C function disappears for references; `Option<&T>` is the type when absence is possible.

Borrowing is also how a function reads data without taking ownership: `fn sum(values: &[i32])` reads the caller's vector and leaves it with the caller. The aliasing bug in the challenge's C original, `append_doubled(v, v->data, v->len)`, cannot be written in Rust: a `&mut dst` and a `&dst` in the same call are rejected.
writing.exampleCaption: The value is copied out before `push`, and `sum` borrows `v` for reading only, so the later `push` is allowed.
writing.task: Port the commented C function: `append_doubled` pushes twice each value of `src` onto the end of `dst` and leaves `src` with the caller.
writing.success: Values are appended after the existing ones, an empty `src` changes nothing, and `src` is still usable after the call.
writing.question: Why does rustc reject `let first = &v[0]; v.push(2); println!("{first}");`?
answers: `first` is a shared borrow still in use when `push` needs a mutable borrow of `v`
`push` takes `v` by value, so `v` has moved
Elements of a vector cannot be borrowed; you must use an index
writing.feedback: The shared borrow lives until the `println!`. Print before pushing, or copy the value out with `let first = v[0];`, and the mutable borrow no longer overlaps it.

recall.question: Does this compile?
recall.answer: Yes, and it prints `1` and `[1, 2, 3]`. The shared borrow `first` is last used in the first `println!`, so it has ended before `push` takes `&mut v`. Borrows last until their last use, not until the end of the scope.

recall.question: What contract does `fn fill(dst: &mut [u8], src: &[u8])` state that the C prototype `void fill(uint8_t *dst, const uint8_t *src, size_t n)` does not?
recall.answer: That `dst` and `src` do not overlap and that each is valid for its own length. A caller cannot pass the same buffer as both, because a `&mut` and a `&` to it cannot coexist. In C that takes `restrict` plus documentation, and nothing checks it.

bridge.fromCaption: `first` points into the old buffer after `realloc`; AddressSanitizer reports a heap use after free.

contrasts.from: Any number of `T *` may read and write at the same time.
contrasts.rust: Many `&T` readers or one `&mut T` writer at a time; a conflict is `E0502`.
`&mut T` is exclusive, and the compiler checks it.

contrasts.from: A pointer may be NULL or dangle; callers check by hand.
contrasts.rust: A reference is never null and cannot outlive its value.
